planting.note: Nick or file the hard seed coat and soak overnight before sowing to speed germination; this selection is bred for necks reaching two to three feet, so a tall overhead trellis is essential for straight handles rather than the curled shapes that form when fruit trails on the ground.

directions: This selection of Lagenaria siceraria is bred specifically for exceptionally long, slender necks that can stretch two to three feet, far exceeding the handle length of a typical dipper gourd. Provide an overhead arbor or fence at least eight feet tall so the developing handle hangs straight down under its own weight instead of curling on the ground. The large white flowers open in early evening and are pollinated mainly by moths, so hand-pollinating with a soft brush at dusk improves fruit set where night pollinators are scarce. Let fruit remain on the vine until the stem shrivels and the shell turns hard, then cure the gourds in a warm, airy space for one to several months until they feel light and the seeds rattle before cleaning and finishing them as dippers or ladles.

planting.note: Direct sow in warm soil after all frost danger passes and let the vine sprawl over open ground rather than climb, since trellising elongates the fruit away from the rounded shape traditionally wanted for hula implements.

directions: This Hawaiian strain of bottle gourd is traditionally grown along the ground rather than on a trellis, which lets the fruit develop the rounder, double-bulbed form prized for carving the ipu heke gourd drum and other hula implements, rather than the elongated shapes that result from vertical training. Give the sprawling vine a generous patch of warm, fertile soil in full sun and water regularly through fruit set. Both a sweeter-fleshed strain historically used for food and a more bitter strain grown strictly for vessels have been selected over centuries, so flavor of immature fruit can vary by seed source. Harvest for craft use only after the fruit fully matures and the stem dries, then cure for several weeks in a dry, ventilated space until the shell hardens completely before hollowing and finishing.

common_name: Jaune Gros de Paris Pumpkin (Yellow of Paris)

planting.note: Direct sow in hills after the soil has warmed past 65°F; this historic French heirloom needs a long, warm season and heavily enriched soil to size up its huge fruit, making the Gulf Coast's extended frost-free window an advantage.

directions: Jaune Gros de Paris is a market-garden heirloom long grown around the French capital, prized for its enormous, flattened, lightly ribbed fruit in soft pastel yellow-pink that can weigh anywhere from 25 to well over 100 pounds. Sow into hills enriched with compost or aged manure and thin to two vigorous vines per hill, allowing plenty of room for the sprawling growth. The deep orange flesh is dense and moderately sweet, well suited to soups, gratins, and baked dishes rather than fresh eating. Harvest once the rind hardens and resists a fingernail, then cure in a warm spot for a couple of weeks before moving to cool, dry storage, where the fruit keeps for several months.

planting.note: Direct sow after last frost in warm soil; this compact, non-vining strain of Buttercup fits raised beds and small plots where a sprawling squash vine would not.

directions: Emerald Bush Buttercup is a compact, short-vined strain selected from classic Buttercup squash, holding the same turban shape and small blossom-end button but on a plant that stays within a few feet rather than running eight feet or more. Give it consistent moisture and full sun; because the foliage is dense and close together, watch for powdery mildew in humid climates and space plants for airflow. Fruit averages about four to five pounds with nearly black-green skin and dry, sweet, deep orange-yellow flesh well suited to baking and mashing. Cure harvested fruit at room temperature for a week or two before moving it to cool, dry storage.

planting.note: Direct sow in hills after soil has warmed; this rare 1880s New England heirloom is a natural turban-Hubbard cross and needs a full warm season to fully harden its thick rind.

directions: Essex Hybrid dates to an 1880s New England seed catalog description as a natural cross between a turban squash and a Hubbard, combining the turban's rounded shape with the Hubbard's tough, heavily warted rind in a bright orange-red skin. Once a popular fall display squash in the Northeast, it faded from commerce and now survives mainly through small heirloom seed savers, so seed can be harder to source than mainstream Hubbard types. Grow it exactly as you would any vining Cucurbita maxima, giving the sprawling plant six to eight feet of room and steady moisture through fruit set. The dense, sweet flesh cooks well for pies and mashing, and the thick, warty rind makes it an excellent long-term keeper once cured.
sources: historical J.J.H. Gregory & Son seed catalog references

planting.note: Direct sow in hills after soil has warmed past 65°F; give this rare 1896 Massachusetts heirloom a full long season, since its exceptionally hard rind takes the entire warm-season window to develop.

directions: Marblehead was introduced in 1896 out of Massachusetts as a selection valued for the stony hardness of its smooth grey-green rind, a trait that earned it the name and made it one of the longest-storing winter squashes of its era. Sow in enriched hills and let the vigorous vine sprawl over six to eight feet, watering steadily through the growing season to size up the large, rounded fruit. The deep orange flesh is fine-grained and flavorful, holding up well in soups and baked dishes even after months of storage. Because the shell is so hard, cure fruit for two to three weeks in a warm spot before moving it to a cool, dry root cellar or pantry, where it can keep considerably longer than thinner-skinned squash.

planting.note: Direct sow once soil is reliably warm; this close relative of ridge gourd bears smooth, non-ribbed fruit in tight clusters rather than the single ribbed fruit typical of common Luffa acutangula.

directions: Satputia is a semi-domesticated relative of ridge gourd, distinct enough to be classified as its own species, valued in parts of northeastern India for bearing several smooth, unribbed young fruit together in a single cluster rather than one at a time along the vine. The plant's hermaphrodite flowers set fruit more readily than typical monoecious luffa, often giving noticeably heavier yields per vine over a shorter, more compact fruiting season. Provide a trellis or fence for the twining vine and harvest fruit young and tender, well before the skin toughens or ribs develop, for use exactly as you would ridge gourd in stir-fries and curries. Because it thrives in hot, humid conditions, it performs especially well through a long, warm Gulf Coast summer.
sources: Springer Nature Genetic Resources and Crop Evolution journal
Indian Society of Vegetable Science (Vegetable Science journal)
